items.title: AI in tourism and hospitality: from predictive infrastructure to experiential interface
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to review the evolution of artificial intelligence (AI) research in tourism and hospitality (T&H), tracing its shift from back-end analytical infrastructure to front-stage experiential interface. This study maps conceptual foundations, thematic dynamics and methodological patterns, with particular attention to generative AI (GenAI), and develops a future research agenda for responsible and sustainability-oriented AI innovation. Design/methodology/approach This study conducted a longitudinal bibliometric and thematic review of 1, 851 peer-reviewed articles (1986–2025) from Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection. Following the PRISMA guidelines, VOSviewer and Gephi were used for co-occurrence and citation mapping, interpreting thematic evolution across four historical phases to inform a theory-driven research agenda. Findings Two trajectories structure the field: AI as analytical infrastructure (optimizing forecasting and decision-making) and AI as experiential interface (facilitating generative, interactive and emotionally embedded service encounters). The field has evolved from symbolic logic and data mining to multimodal analytics, service robots and GenAI applications. The proposed agenda highlights methodological transparency, ethical and accountable AI, human–AI collaboration, employee welfare and sustainable transformation. Originality/value This study offers a structured, theory-informed synthesis of AI research in T&H. By linking historical trajectories with emerging priorities, it helps scholars, practitioners and policymakers understand where AI creates value, where risks arise and how future T&H research can respond to the GenAI era.

items.title: AI Innovative Practical Teaching Model for Interdisciplinary Postgraduates Integrated with OBE Concept
items.abstract: Traditional postgraduate education faces challenges in personalized guidance, dynamic competency tracking, and interdisciplinary practical training. This study proposed an AI-driven practical teaching model for interdisciplinary postgraduates based on the Outcomes-Based Education (OBE) concept. We adopted AI-assisted English learning as a representative application scenario and constructed a closed-loop teaching framework that integrates multi-agent collaboration, Large Language Models (LLM), and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The framework establishes a multidimensional learner state model and a learning benefit function to support dynamic learner modeling, personalized task allocation, and intelligent feedback. We conducted a ten-week classroom teaching experiment involving interdisciplinary postgraduate students. The experiment compared three modes: traditional instruction, AI-agent-supported learning, and the integrated RAG–LLM teaching framework. The experimental results show that the proposed framework improves learning-path stability, and promote balanced development of vocabulary, grammar, listening, and speaking abilities. It also enhances the effectiveness and interpretability of feedback. The integrated RAG–LLM architecture facilitates the transition from passive learning to active learning. It also strengthens learner autonomy and strategic decision-making. This study provides an OBE-oriented AI teaching framework that integrate multi-agent collaboration with LLM and RAG technologies. The framework offers practical guidance for intelligent education and interdisciplinary postgraduate training.

items.title: AI literacy and vocational students’ complex problem-solving skills: a moderated mediation model of systematic thinking, cognitive load, and perceived school ICT support
items.abstract: As technological advancements such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshape the landscape of work, career development in vocational education is increasingly oriented toward dynamic, long-term personal growth. In this context, Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) have become a critical competence, reflecting students’ capacity to address ill-structured tasks and adapt to rapidly changing environments. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the relationship between AI Literacy and students’ self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) in higher vocational colleges and the cognitive pathways that may help explain this relationship. This study posits that AI Literacy, as a personal agentic factor, is positively associated with self-reported CPS both directly and indirectly through Systematic Thinking Skills and cognitive load, and that perceived school information and communication technology (ICT) support may condition the strength of these associations. To provide temporal separation among the focal measures, a multi-wave survey was administered to 784 students from six higher vocational institutions at three time points. Data were analyzed using SPSS and Mplus. Results indicated that AI Literacy was significantly associated with self-reported CPS, with significant indirect effects estimated through Systematic Thinking Skills and the six-item cognitive-load composite. Notably, the associations between AI Literacy and these cognitive factors were stronger at higher levels of perceived school ICT support. These findings highlight the relevance of AI Literacy and students’ perceptions of ICT support to self-reported CPS and their preparation for AI-integrated workplaces.

items.title: AI Provenance and the Evaluation of Intellectual Work: Rational Risk, Social Meaning, and Human–AI Performance
items.abstract: AI can improve a piece of intellectual work while knowledge of its use can reduce the credit or trust that the work receives. Understanding that possibility requires separating what AI did to performance from what disclosure adds to evaluation. We connect these questions by asking what the evaluator intends to assess. Improvement relative to a producer’s unaided baseline may matter when the objective is better output; a different benchmark is needed when the objective is to measure unaided capability, assign intellectual credit, or allocate opportunities. A binary “AI was used” label supplies little information about those distinctions. Its relevance depends on the function AI performed, the authority the human retained, verification, and the object of evaluation. Negative reactions may reflect expected error or checking cost, an institutional requirement, social meanings concerning effort and authenticity, or a combination of these explanations. We examine how evidence can distinguish them without treating every penalty as stigma. We then follow evaluation back into production: anticipated disclosure can change whether and how people use AI, including whether they forgo useful assistance. As technology and institutions evolve, the practical question remains whether provenance-based treatment serves the evaluation’s stated purpose or substitutes a category judgment for more direct evidence.

items.title: AI-Assisted Imaging for Suspected Adolescent Endometriosis: Perspectives from Qualitative Focus Groups
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted imaging may support recognition of endometriosis, but perspectives on its use in adolescent care remain unclear. This study explored young people, parents, and health professionals’ views on its potential benefits, acceptable roles, perceived risks, and safeguards. Methods: Four semi-structured focus groups were conducted with adolescents aged 14–17 years (n = 3), young adults aged 18–25 years (n = 9), parents or carers (n = 5), and health professionals (n = 13). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Results: Four themes were developed: (1) diagnostic support, (2) human–AI collaboration, (3) automation bias and diagnostic harm, and (4) responsible AI use. Participants were cautiously hopeful that AI could improve image quality, identify subtle or missed findings, and reduce interpretive variation, but supported it only as an adjunct to skilled clinical care. They feared that apparently objective negative outputs could create false reassurance, reinforce diagnostic dismissal, and restrict further investigation. Trust depended on adolescent-relevant validation, representative data, transparent communication and consent, clear accountability, and clinicians retaining the expertise and authority to question or override AI outputs. Conclusion: AI-assisted imaging should strengthen rather than replace clinical judgment, and a negative AI-assisted imaging result should not prevent further assessment when symptoms persist.

items.title: AI-associated linguistic shifts in Swedish university theses: a corpus-level analysis, 2020–2025
items.abstract: Surveys document widespread student use of generative AI, yet corpus-level evidence of how post-ChatGPT thesis writing has changed remains scarce. We analysed approximately 17,000 Swedish bachelor's and master's theses from six universities, spanning the release of ChatGPT (2020–2025), scoring each on five language dimensions with OpenAI's gpt-4o-mini and grouping them into six topical clusters. Across the corpus, four writing-quality dimensions — grammar, vocabulary, academic quality, and wordiness — rose together after 2022, a modest but statistically clear change of trend that coincides with the release rather than continuing any earlier drift. The shift was present in every discipline, including fields that the published-research literature does not flag, and its disciplinary ordering was inverted relative to that literature: theses in Sustainability and Society changed most, those in Informatics and Engineering least. The rater's own AI-likelihood judgment, by contrast, proved unreliable — it rated more polished writing as less likely to be AI-generated, the opposite of what AI-text detection assumes, and was structurally miscalibrated against its own language-quality scores. Taken together, the results point to a linguistic shift consistent with AI-influenced writing across Swedish thesis prose, while cautioning that the direct AI-likelihood signal cannot be trusted and that analyses of this kind should rest on the language-quality dimensions instead.

items.title: AI-Based Hybrid Deep Learning Framework for Accurate Brain Tumor Classification from MRI Images Using CNN and Vision Transformer
items.abstract: Brain tumors remain among the most life-threatening neurological disorders, and their outcome depends heavily on how early and how accurately they are diagnosed. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for tumor evaluation, yet manual reading of MRI scans is slow and subject to inter-observer disagreement. This paper proposes NeuroFusionNet, a lightweight hybrid deep learning framework that fuses a MobileNetV2-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) branch with a Vision Transformer (ViT) branch through a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) gated fusion mechanism, allowing the model to combine fine-grained local texture cues with long-range global context in a single forward pass. The framework further incorporates a U-Net-based segmentation head to delineate tumor boundaries, a five-method Explainable AI (XAI) suite for transparent decision support, and a Large Language Model (LLM) module that converts model outputs into structured, human-readable clinical reports. Evaluated on the BRISC 2025 benchmark, which contains expert-annotated MRI scans spanning glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and healthy classes, the proposed model achieves 96.2% test accuracy while using only 7.8 million parameters, indicating that competitive diagnostic accuracy can be obtained without the computational burden typical of large-scale transformer or ensemble models. The results suggest that NeuroFusionNet is a practical candidate for deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings that still require interpretable, end-to-end decision support.

items.title: AI-Based Mobile Phone Screen Defect Detection Using OpenCV, YOLO, and Convolutional Neural Networks
items.abstract: Mobile phone screens are essential components of modern smartphones and may develop defects such as cracks,scratches, dark spots, and surface damage. Manual inspection can be time-consuming and may produce inconsistent results under changing lighting conditions. This paper presents a proposed artificial intelligence-based framework for automated mobile phone screen defect detection using OpenCV, You Only Look Once (YOLO), and convolutional neural networks (CNNs). OpenCV supports image acquisition and preprocessing, while YOLO is used to detect potential defects and estimate their locations. A CNN-based classifier may be incorporated when separate classification of detected regions is required. The system is designed to report defect categories, bounding boxes, and confidence scores, as well as indicate when no defect is detected above a selected threshold. The proposed framework describes the processing pipeline, system architecture, and evaluation strategy. Its effectiveness must be established through implementation and testing on a representative, accurately annotated dataset. items.title: AI-Driven Corporate Decision-Making and Directors' Fiduciary Duties: Can an Algorithm Replace the Boardroom?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyse corporate data, forecast commercial outcomes, identify compliance risks and rank strategic alternatives. These capabilities can improve the speed and breadth of board-level analysis, but they also raise a fundamental question of company law: when an algorithm materially influences a corporate decision, who remains accountable for the outcome? This paper examines that question principally through section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013, which requires directors to act in good faith, exercise care, skill and diligence, and apply independent judgment. It argues that AI may support directors but cannot displace their fiduciary role. The central distinction is between using a system as an analytical aid and allowing its output to become a substitute for genuine deliberation. The paper considers automation bias, limited explainability, data quality, vendor dependence and the risk of fragmented accountability. It then draws carefully bounded lessons from the European Union’s AI regulatory framework and Indian financial regulation, before proposing governance measures concerning material-use disclosure, board competence, meaningful explanations, documentation, validation and continuing human responsibility. The paper concludes that corporate governance can become increasingly algorithm-assisted, but the legal responsibility for corporate judgment must remain traceable to accountable human decision-makers.

items.abstract: Advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and health care analytics has provided novel ways to personalize healthcare and implement precision medicine. This study suggests developing an AI-based personalized healthcare system based on analysis of patients' demographic details, health care history, lab results, genomic information, and current health parameters to predict their disease risks and make personalized treatment decisions. For implementation of this concept, machine learning models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, Support Vector Machine, and neural network will be applied to analyze various data related to health care and identify patterns related to disease development and its treatment. Predictive analysis will be performed to determine patients' risk scores, probability of disease and treatment outcomes. Moreover, the use of explainable AI will enhance the transparency of predictions made. The proposed system will aim at 90-95% accuracy of predictions, about 30-40% decrease in time required to make diagnostics decisions and about 25-35% better early-risk detection than traditional approaches.

items.abstract: The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and Natural Language Processing (NLP) has expanded the use of automated techniques for resume analysis, recruitment matching, job recommendation, skill development, and interview preparation.This paper presents a comprehensive review of existing research on AIdriven resume analysis and placement support across five interconnected research areas: resume intelligence; semantic matching and Applicant Tracking System (ATS) evaluation; career and skill development; Large Language Model (LLM) and conversational support; and interview intelligence.The reviewed studies employ traditional NLP and machinelearning techniques such as regular expressions (regex), keyword matching, Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF), Bag-of-Words (BoW), Word to Vector (Word2Vec), cosine similarity, k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Logistic Regression and fuzzy logic, together with Named Entity Recognition (NER), Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), Robustly Optimized BERT Pretraining Approach (RoBERTa), distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (DistilBERT), attention-based neural networks, collaborative filtering, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and LLM-based architectures.The literature shows a methodological progression from lexical and rule-based processing toward contextual, semantic, and generative approaches, with several studies reporting strong task-specific performance.At the same time, the evidence remains functionally fragmented: resume parsing and matching are extensively studied, while ATS evaluation, skill-gap analysis, learning support, conversational assistance, and AI-based interview preparation are addressed by smaller and more specialized groups of studies.The review identifies an integration gap in the literature, together with limitations related to dataset diversity, evaluation comparability, changing job requirements, explainability, fairness, privacy, and real-world validation.The findings provide a consolidated view of current methods, reported outcomes, and research opportunities in AI-supported resume analysis and placement preparation.

items.title: AI-Empowered Value Co-Creation for Intangible Cultural Heritage Digital Revitalization: A Conceptual Multi-Case Analysis
items.abstract: The digital revitalization of intangible cultural heritage (ICH) is central to China’s national strategy for digital culture. Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping how ICH is safeguarded, transmitted, and innovated. Yet most studies focus on technological applications and have not systematically theorized how AI enters ICH value co-creation. Drawing on value co-creation theory, this study develops an analytical framework. It applies the framework through a conceptual multi-case analysis of eight publicly accessible online cases spanning different ICH domains and lead actors. Cross-case comparison tests the framework’s explanatory power. The findings identify four dominant models of ICH value co-creation under AI: heritage-bearer-led human-machine co-creation, public-platform-based crowd co-creation and benefit sharing, business-driven value monetization, and government-led ecosystem synergy. Multiple actors advance ICH digital revitalization through resource co-creation, production co-creation, experience co-creation, and value sharing, and AI shifts from an instrumental tool to a collaborative partner. The study extends value co-creation theory and offers an analytical tool for ICH digital revitalization.

items.title: AI-enabled drug repurposing in Alzheimer’s disease: from computational nomination to pharmacological proof
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has expanded the scale and speed of drug repurposing in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Transcriptomic signature matching, network-based systems pharmacology, real-world data pharmacoepidemiology and multi-omics machine learning have generated hundreds of candidate drugs, while repurposed agents account for 35% (56 of 158) of drugs and 42% (15 of 36) of Phase 3 agents in the 2026 AD pipeline. Clinical translation, however, remains unproven. Randomised trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists illustrate the gap between prioritisation and therapeutic proof: semaglutide did not slow clinical progression in evoke and evoke+, while liraglutide did not improve the primary FDG-PET endpoint in ELAD. We examine four complementary evidence domains, defining what each can and cannot establish, and position large language models as a cross-cutting tool for evidence synthesis and knowledge-graph reasoning rather than an independent source of biological evidence. Rather than cataloguing methods and candidates, we appraise leading drugs at the individual-molecule level and propose explicit criteria for progression from computational nomination to clinical testing. The framework defines seven requirements for clinical progression: disease-stage matching, adequate site-of-action exposure, including CNS exposure for central mechanisms, mechanistic validation in human-relevant models, biomarker-stratified trial design, convergence across independent evidence domains, causal inference with explicit boundary conditions, and mechanism-aligned endpoints with predefined stopping rules. AI has improved candidate prioritisation in AD, but clinical value will depend on converting ranked hypotheses into pharmacologically plausible and prospectively testable programmes.

items.title: AI-Powered Swagger/OpenAPI Developer Assistant
items.abstract: Application Programming Interface (API) specifications written in the Swagger/OpenAPI format are the primary reference for developers who consume RESTful services, yet large specifications are time-consuming to read, cannot be queried in natural language, and must be tested and documented using separate tools. This paper presents the AI-Powered Swagger/OpenAPI Developer Assistant, a web-based platform that unifies these activities in a single workspace. A developer uploads a specification in JSON or YAML format; a Spring Boot back end parses it into structured endpoint information and supplies it as context to the Google Gemini large language model, which answers natural-language questions about endpoints, authentication, parameters, request and response schemas and error codes. The platform further provides an interactive API playground that builds request forms from the specification, executes live requests through a server-side executor and explains the returned response, together with a documentation generator for single endpoints or the complete API. The user interface is implemented in React with TypeScript. The paper describes the architecture, design decisions, implementation and security considerations of the system and discusses its advantages and limitations compared with a conventional multi-tool workflow.

items.title: AIoT Fault Diagnosis Maintenance Frameworks Based Metaheuristic and Two‐Stage Deep Learning Algorithms for Diesel Generators
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Background The reliable operation of diesel generators, which are critical devices in many industrial applications in maintaining continuous power supply, is essential. Objective This research presents an advanced Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) fault diagnosis framework that combines metaheuristic optimization and two‐stage deep learning methods to improve the fault classification accuracy of diesel generators. Methods The improved particle swarm optimization (IPSO) is used to fine‐tune the hyperparameters of bidirectional long short‐term memories (BiLSTM) combined with convolutional neural networks (CNN). The developed hybrid model aims to exploit the power of both the sequential learning of BiLSTMs and the feature extraction capability of CNNs to achieve superior fault diagnosis performance. Seven established baselines provide the point of reference for the IPSO‐BiLSTM‐CNN framework: recurrent neural network (RNN), CNN, gated recurrent unit (GRU), LSTM, bidirectional RNN (BiRNN), BiLSTM and CNN‐BiLSTM. Results Experimental results demonstrate that IPSO‐BiLSTM‐CNN methods outperform existing models in terms of accuracy and stability, achieving relative reductions of 71.56% in loss, 73.79% validating loss, 64.63% mean absolute error (MAE), 69.75% validating MAE, 23.17% cosine proximity (CP), 21.99% validating CP, 63.08% mean squared error (MSE), 71.55% validating MSE, together with relative improvements of 4.79% precision (PRE), 3.79% validating PRE, 5.8% recall (REC), and 5.29% validating REC. Conclusions This highlights its potential in practical AIoT applications for diesel generator monitoring and maintenance.

items.title: Algorithmic Bias Concerns and Acceptance of AI Supported Legal Decision Making in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence can assist legal work while creating risks of discrimination, opaque reasoning and diminished accountability. This study examines whether concern about biased training data coexists with perceived usefulness and support for safeguards among respondents to a Bangladesh legal-AI survey. The analysis uses 385 adult, AI-aware survey records supplied by the research team. Because the questionnaire combines risk perceptions, utility and governance preferences, the analysis retains individual items rather than presenting the blocks as validated scales. Descriptive distributions, paired endorsement comparisons and exploratory Spearman correlations assess distinct aspects of the research question. Concern about biased training data was endorsed by 334 respondents (86.8%), regular audits by 317 (82.3%) and a right to review or appeal by 328 (85.2%). AI assistance with organising information was endorsed by 247 (64.2%); 219 (56.9%) endorsed both this usefulness item and bias concern. The rank correlation between bias concern and perceived usefulness was small (ρ = .075), with no clear evidence of association after adjustment for multiple comparisons. These self-reported attitudes cannot establish the fairness of a system, causal effects or the actual conditions under which a respondent would rely on an AI recommendation. The results point to the importance of measuring perceived benefits, risk and procedural protections separately. The article integrates technology acceptance and procedural justice as a framework for future scenario-based studies and proposes proportionate auditing, meaningful human review and accessible contestation for legal decision support.

items.title: Algorithmic Constitutionalism in Mexico: Artificial Intelligence, Public Power, and the Transformation of Fundamental Rights
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the scope of state action in the area of basic rights.AI use by public institutions is reshaping the scope of state action in the area of basic rights. This research aimed thus to evaluate the sufficiency of the Mexican constitution to control the use of AI by public bodies and to propose a model of algorithmic constitutionalism. A qualitative and documentary study was carried out in the field of algorithmic governance, reviewing constitutional norms, Mexican jurisprudence, academic studies and international instruments on issues such as transparency and explainability, human oversight and the protection of rights. The outcome shows that there are some bases for the regulation of automated decision making that are provided in the Mexican Constitution, specifically in the sections related to equality, data protection, access to information, due process and effective judicial protection. The regulatory landscape is divided and does not include a classification of risks, impact assessment, auditing or procedures to challenge algorithm decisions. Therefore, a democratic algorithmic constitutionalism model is presented, which is based on legal authorization, proportionality, transparency, explainability, human control, non-discrimination, judicial control, and accountability.

items.title: Algorithmic Postmodernism: A Framework
items.abstract: Algorithmic Postmodernism is a conceptual framework originated by Hoang-Dan Pham, conceived in 2024 with the founding of Hand-Fetish-Projects and formally stated in 2026. It describes a condition in which visibility increasingly precedes interpretation: search engines, recommendation systems and artificial-intelligence-based indexing decide what reaches attention before any person has encountered it, and so shape the conditions under which cultural value is recognised. It also takes a position: human beings should retain the power to decide what matters. Algorithmic Postmodernism is not a claim of total system control, and it takes no stance for or against artificial intelligence. Its specific contribution is to name a judge that evaluates each work from its own context, not from the context in which the work was made: a function with an authored goal and no authored rule. It locates that judge in art, the field built entirely on judging whether something deserves attention. The framework emerged from the practice of Hand-Fetish-Projects, an independent arthouse, and is positioned here against Lyotard, Baudrillard, Deleuze, Wiener and Doctorow.

items.title: Alpha: Systematic Fault Injection and Robustness Evaluation for LLM-Driven Embodied Manipulation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.

items.title: An Adaptive Learning Framework for Educational Product Innovation
items.abstract: Digital learning increasingly combines platforms, artificial intelligence, multiple content formats, and social distribution, yet these elements are often designed as separate tools. This paper develops a conceptual framework for educational product innovation that connects these elements into an adaptive learning ecosystem. The study uses a conceptual synthesis approach. A focused synthesis of peer-reviewed literature and policy guidance on AI in education, adaptive learning, digital ecosystems, formative assessment, and social-media-supported learning was combined with a structured analysis of the framework and practical implementation examples documented in the author's 2026 monograph. The implementation examples are treated as illustrative cases rather than as an empirical evaluation. The resulting framework identifies three interacting infrastructure layers, digital products and platforms, artificial intelligence, and social distribution, and seven linked design processes: defining the learning need, packaging knowledge, building an owned digital home, augmenting with AI, designing the attention path, creating feedback loops, and measuring, learning and iterating. The framework integrates access, personalisation, engagement, assessment, and continuous improvement within one architecture. The framework offers a practical conceptual model for educators, learning designers, and education entrepreneurs developing technology-enabled learning experiences. It extends technology-centred approaches by treating distribution and feedback as integral parts of the learning ecosystem. Future research should empirically test the framework across educational settings and examine learner outcomes, equity, privacy, and sustainability.

items.title: An Explainable Hybrid AI–Gamification Framework for Adaptive E-Learning Systems with Simulation-Based Validation
items.abstract: Gamified e-learning platforms and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven adaptive learning systems can improve learner engagement, but existing solutions rarely combine the two, and few explain their adaptive decisions to learners. To address this gap, we propose LearnSpace, a hybrid AI–gamification framework for responsive e-learning that adds an Explanation Layer, based on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), to a deterministic reward architecture. The framework merges classical gamification mechanics with an AI personalization module in which experience points, rewards, and difficulty adjustments follow explicit weighted formulas. A Thompson-sampling bandit learns which feedback works best after a mistake. For each adaptive decision, the Explanation Layer names only the factors that drive it and turns them into a short justification for the learner. The design draws on a qualitative overview of 14 platforms, and the LearnSpace mobile prototype implements the gamification components and the bandit. In a pre-registered simulation with 500 synthetic learners per run, the first explanation rule named a factor that had no effect on the decision in 95.3% of difficulty adjustments, while the decision-specific rule never did. The bandit had lower regret than uniformly random feedback allocation. Effects on real learners remain to be tested.

items.title: An Explainable Zero-Trust Framework for Detecting Generative-AI-Enhanced Phishing and Credential Theft Using Real-World Threat Data
items.abstract: Phishing has evolved from simple fraudulent messages into a multi-channel credential-theft ecosystem thatcombines malicious URLs, QR-code phishing, adversary-in-the-middle proxying, business e-mail compromise,deepfake-assisted social engineering, and generative-AI-assisted content generation. This paper proposes anexplainable zero-trust framework for detecting and reducing phishing-related credential exposure using real-worldthreat intelligence and the PhiUSIIL public benchmark dataset. The study integrates APWG observations from2024 through Q3 2025 with a benchmark containing 235,795 URLs, 54 variables, 134,850 legitimate samples,and 100,945 phishing samples. The framework combines URL and page-content features, brand-mismatch evi-dence, QR-code detonation, sender-authentication signals, phishing-resistant MFA, conditional access, browserisolation, and human-readable explanations. A supervised benchmark experiment was conducted using a singlestratified 80/20 train-test split and three baseline classifiers. Decision Tree achieved 100.00% F1-score, RandomForest achieved 99.9975% F1-score, and Gaussian Naive Bayes achieved 98.1923% F1-score on the held-outtest set. These single-split benchmark results support a layered conclusion: URL detection is useful, but strongerrisk reduction is achieved when detection, identity, isolation, reporting, and continuous governance operate asone zero-trust system.

items.title: An Interactive Assistant to Support Security Operators
items.abstract: The security of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) is paramount, yet human operators frequently face cognitive overload when managing complex cyber-physical threats. This chapter presents a comprehensive overview of AVATAR4BC, a novel, personalized Intelligent Virtual Assistant (IVA) designed to address this critical human-factors challenge. Our system represents a paradigm shift from traditional dashboards by providing an embodied, conversational interface that leverages a high-fidelity 3D human avatar. A core contribution of AVATAR4BC is its multidisciplinary approach, which goes beyond technical integration. It fuses advanced Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) with insights from the Social Sciences and Humanities (SSH). The system’s backend integrates Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), and real-time speech-driven facial animation to create a natural interaction. Crucially, it incorporates Explainable AI (XAI) principles by using Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate human-readable explanations of opaque Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) agent decisions from the underlying DYNABIC framework. Furthermore, AVATAR4BC’s personalization engine, informed by psychological and behavioral research, dynamically adapts the avatar’s appearance, voice, and communication style to the operator, aiming to reduce stress and enhance decision-making effectiveness. Final validation through end-to-end unit testing demonstrates the system’s core functionality, confirming the seamless integration of its architectural components. This work establishes a robust foundation for future research into human–AI collaboration, with significant implications for enhancing resilience in cybersecurity and other high-stakes domains.

items.title: Application and Optimization of Multimodal Knowledge Management in Web-Based English Teaching
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of digital transformation, English teaching is constrained by over-reliance on single-modal resources and insufficient integration of web technologies and pedagogy, which hinder the development of learners' higher-order skills. Using mixed-methods research, this study constructs a cognition-centered multimodal knowledge management framework based on cognitive load theory. It develops a system for resource classification, scenario adaptation, and cognitive activation alongside a three-dimensional tagging mechanism and an augmented reality‒supported technology-teaching double-helix model. Proper visual‒auditory input matching facilitates learners' information retention. Empirical evaluation reveals positive changes in classroom group interaction, digital tool adoption, and students' written logical performance. This study offers practical optimization strategies and suggests bridging the digital divide, strengthening teachers' technological pedagogical content knowledge capability, and exploring artificial intelligence applications for web-based multimodal English teaching.

items.abstract: This article analyzes the possibilities of applying modern digital technologies in solar energy systems. It examines the potential of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), Digital Twin, Edge AI, cloud computing, Big Data, blockchain, drones, robotic maintenance, GIS, SCADA, smart inverters, and AR/VR technologies to improve the efficiency of solar photovoltaic power plants, forecast electricity generation, detect technical faults at an early stage, and optimize energy flow management. The article also highlights promising directions, including AI-based Digital Twins, Edge AI, federated learning, autonomous drone inspection, and blockchain-based peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading.

items.title: Applications of Geographic Information Systems in Natural-Resource Management: A Critical Review of Methods, Evidence, Validation and Future Directions
items.abstract: Natural-resource management (NRM) increasingly depends on spatially explicit evidence because land, soil, water, forests and vegetation vary across space and change through time. Geographic Information Systems (GIS), often integrated with remote sensing (RS), provide a common analytical environment for resource inventory, multi-layer integration, change detection, suitability assessment and decision support. This review synthesises a curated corpus of 20 records representing 19 unique studies published between 1995 and 2026; one duplicated Kumar, Yamaç and Velmurugan record was removed before synthesis. The evidence was organised into six domains: (i) planning, decision support and participatory GIS; (ii) multi-sector RS–GIS applications; (iii) soil resources and land degradation; (iv) land-use/land-cover (LULC) change, forests and watershed programmes; (v) water and groundwater; and (vi) agriculture, climate and crop modelling. Across the corpus, overlay analysis, terrain analysis and multi-temporal change detection are the most recurrent GIS functions. Empirical evidence is strongly concentrated in Indian watershed studies. Reported LULC classification accuracies in three case-study groups range from 89.70% to approximately 95%, although these values are not directly comparable because imagery, class schemes and validation designs differ. The synthesis identifies persistent weaknesses in data quality and spatial resolution, field validation, uncertainty reporting, generalisability, subjective weighting in multi-criteria decision-making, limited temporal density, and unequal technical access. Fifteen of the 19 studies explicitly point towards artificial intelligence or machine learning as an emerging opportunity, while UAV/LiDAR data, IoT observations, cloud processing, predictive modelling and participatory web/mobile GIS remain underused. We argue that the next generation of GIS-based NRM should move from static and retrospective mapping towards dynamic, field-validated, uncertainty-aware, predictive and participatory decision systems. A validation-centred framework and a prioritised research agenda are proposed.

items.title: Applying Disability and Equality Law in Occupational Health Practice
items.abstract: This chapter explains how United Kingdom disability and equality law applies within occupational health practice. It introduces disability through the social model and outlines current patterns of work-related ill health, including the increasing prevalence of long-term conditions and the impact of common mental health problems on participation in work. This context supports understanding of the Equality Act 2010 and how it protects individuals whose physical or mental impairments have a substantial and long-term effect on normal day-to-day activities. The chapter summarises the forms of disability discrimination most relevant to employment, including direct discrimination, indirect discrimination, discrimination arising from disability, associative discrimination, harassment and victimisation. It explains the employer’s duty to make reasonable adjustments and illustrates how this duty is interpreted using key legal cases. Building on this framework, the chapter presents a structured approach to assessing disability during fitness-to-work consultations. A worked example demonstrates how functional impact, risk, prognosis and clinical evidence inform clear and defensible recommendations. The chapter concludes with medico-legal principles for high-quality occupational health reporting.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Acceptance Among Nurses and Other Healthcare Professionals in Spain and Henan Province, China: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Comparison
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Assessing artificial intelligence (AI) acceptance may help identify questions for nursing education, but similar overall scores need not reflect similar response patterns. We compared general AI acceptance in healthcare professional samples from Spain and Henan Province, China, including a substantial nursing subgroup. Methods: This exploratory cross-sectional comparison used data from two convenience-sampled online surveys involving 7187 respondents (Spain, 3764; Henan, 3423), including 3590 nurses. We examined a five-item acceptance composite using ordinal confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance testing, observed and adjusted comparisons, and equivalence testing with bounds of ±0.20 pooled standard deviations. Results: Observed means were 3.59 in Spain and 3.56 in Henan; the difference of 0.028 points fell within the exploratory equivalence bounds (90% CI −0.010 to 0.067; bounds ±0.195), whose practical significance has not been established. Metric and scalar constraints met change-in-fit criteria, although absolute fit was mixed and strict invariance was not supported. The scalar model yielded an exploratory latent Henan–Spain contrast of 0.227 reference-group standard deviations (95% CI 0.152 to 0.302), which requires caution given the mixed model fit. The adjusted composite difference was 0.114 points (95% CI 0.054 to 0.173). Item-level differences ran in opposing directions. In the exploratory nursing subgroup analysis, the adjusted Henan–Spain difference was 0.081 points (95% CI −0.014 to 0.176; Holm-adjusted p = 0.283). The interval included zero and positive differences; nurse-specific equivalence was not tested. Conclusions: Similar observed averages concealed heterogeneous responses in these samples. The findings support examining distinct aspects of acceptance when designing nursing-focused needs assessments, not assuming competence or readiness for a particular AI tool. Non-probability recruitment and incomplete cross-cultural validation limit generalization and interpretation. Registration: The study was not registered.

items.title: Artificial intelligence applications in forensic science and their implications for education and training
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly relevant to forensic practice and has potential applications in forensic education, including evidence interpretation, simulation-based learning, and decision-making. Then, evidence regarding its educational implementation remains fragmented, with limited consensus on pedagogical frameworks and competency development. Methodology A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA guidelines. Studies published between 2020 and 2025 were identified through Scopus, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore. Eligible studies for the primary synthesis were required to include an identifiable forensic educational or training context, an AI-supported educational intervention, or a measured educational/training outcome. Technical studies of AI applications in forensic practice were analyzed separately to identify emerging competency and curriculum requirements. Results Only a limited subset of the retrieved literature directly examined AI within an educational or training context. The available educational evidence addressed areas such as learner skill development, professional training needs, and AI-supported learning activities, but remained heterogeneous and methodologically limited. In contrast, a much larger body of technical forensic AI research demonstrated rapid advances in image analysis, classification, digital forensics, and decision support. These developments identify emerging educational requirements in algorithmic literacy, validation, explainability, bias assessment, data governance, and human oversight. Discussion Current evidence indicates that AI should complement rather than replace human expertise. Effective implementation requires competency-based curricula integrating computational literacy, ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary collaboration, and experiential learning supported by explainable AI. Conclusion Direct empirical evidence supporting AI-enhanced forensic education remains limited. This scarcity represents an important evidence gap. Rapid technical advances nevertheless provide a strong rationale for developing and prospectively evaluating competency-based AI education in forensic curricula.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as the More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) 2.0: metadata-driven adaptive scaffolding for narrative comprehension
items.abstract: Introduction Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, yet much of this progress remains focused on answer generation rather than theoretically grounded instructional support. This study introduces AI as the More Knowledgeable Other (MKO) 2.0 , an MKO-inspired framework for generating task-sensitive scaffolds from structured question metadata. Methods Using the Quest Dataset of 6,989 narrative-comprehension questions, a rule-based system operationalized three task dimensions, comprehension attribute, explicit/implicit evidence status, and local/summary scope, into seven primary scaffold families and 28 surface realizations. An attribute-stratified sample of 140 questions was subsequently used to compare rule-based scaffolds with generic narrative-grounded and MKO-conditioned LLM scaffolds. Findings Across paired LLM outputs, MKO-conditioned scaffolds were more elaborated than generic scaffolds, averaging 5.18 additional words per instance ( W = 356.5, p < 0.001), and showed slightly higher corpus-level lexical variation (MATTR-50 = 0.785 vs. 0.765). Narrative-evidence cues occurred more frequently under MKO conditioning (40.0% vs. 10.0%, p < 0.001), while, among implicit questions, inference-oriented cues occurred in 36.1% of MKO-conditioned scaffolds compared with 2.8% of generic scaffolds ( p =0.002). In contrast, question-specific reference did not differ significantly, and MKO conditioning did not reduce lexical answer overlap. Discussion These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using structured task metadata to organize AI-generated scaffolding and show that metadata conditioning is associated with measurable differences in scaffold realization. The study contributes a transparent, task-sensitive framework for shifting AI-supported learning from answer provision toward structured guidance, while recognizing that learner-level pedagogical effectiveness requires direct human evaluation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for intimate apparel fit and comfort from technical evidence to business governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for intimate apparel supports body measurement, size and product recommendation, garment simulation, and virtual try-on, but these tasks provide different evidence about fit and comfort. This critical narrative review examines direct bra research alongside adjacent apparel technologies and identifies the validation needed for business use. Recent direct studies include machine-learning models of breast morphology, bra recommendation prototypes, finite-element contact models, dynamic scanning, pressure measurements, and longitudinal wearer research. They establish meaningful component-level progress, while leaving uncertainty about transfer across products and populations and about the causal effects of AI-assisted decisions on customer and financial outcomes. Two-dimensional image quality, three-dimensional geometric agreement, physical support, perceived comfort, and business impact are therefore evaluated separately. An operational transfer test distinguishes methodological relevance from evidence of successful domain transfer. Building on the evidence gaps, the review proposes task-specific evaluation priorities, safeguards for intimate body data, and a staged research agenda with explicit resource and decision requirements. These proposals are analytical contributions, not empirically validated maturity models or deployment guarantees. The central implication is that businesses should match each proposed claim to its measured outcome and scale investment only after the relevant technical, wearer, and operational evidence is established.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Marine Functional Peptide Discovery: Challenges, Advances, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Marine organisms represent a rich but underexplored source of bioactive peptides with potential applications in therapeutics, nutraceuticals, and biotechnology. However, conventional marine peptide discovery relies on labor-intensive workflows involving specimen collection, extraction, purification, structural characterization, and experimental validation, limiting the efficient exploration of the rapidly expanding marine sequence space. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) provide new opportunities to accelerate peptide discovery by enabling large-scale sequence analysis, functional prediction, and candidate prioritization. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-driven marine functional peptide discovery, covering peptide resources, computational representations, machine-learning and deep-learning methods, protein language models, generative approaches, genome and metagenome mining, and structure-aware prediction strategies. We further discuss representative applications involving marine microorganisms, animal proteomes, cyanobacterial biosynthetic pathways, metagenomic datasets, and marine-derived peptide candidates, highlighting current achievements and limitations. Finally, we analyze key challenges and future perspectives, including marine-specific datasets, multimodal AI models integrating sequence, structural, chemical, and biosynthetic information, rigorous benchmarking, and computational–experimental integration. This review provides a comprehensive framework for understanding how AI can support the discovery and development of functional peptides from marine resources.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for predictive surveillance of Infectious Disease Outbreaks
items.abstract: The rising rate and speed of spread of infectious disease outbreaks require surveillance systems that precede traditional reporting flows. In this paper, we conduct a systematic exploration of the design, development, and assessment of a predictive surveillance framework based on artificial intelligence technologies for outbreak detection and short-term forecasting. The suggested approach entails the integration of multiple types of data sources – open source epidemic intelligence, syndromic data, mobility data, and climatic variables – into a unified pipeline encompassing natural language processing for event extraction, machine learning ensembles for risk classification, and temporal deep learning for trajectory forecasting. An AI framework involving Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) technology for signal classification and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) network for case forecasting is described in algorithmic pseudocode and illustrated via system diagrams. Retrospective analysis in multiple outbreak cases indicates that the ensembling technique yields better discrimination than single-model approaches, whereas the GRU model decreases forecast error in early outbreak growth stages. Results are summarized in a comparative table of different models' configurations. We conclude the paper with an identification of practical hurdles in the deployment of an AI-based surveillance system and the consideration of governance strategies for such systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Biotechnology: Current Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a transformative technology in biotechnology, offering innovative approaches to biological research, healthcare, pharmaceutical development, and industrial applications. The integration of AI techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and generative AI, enables the rapid analysis of complex biological data and supports efficient decision-making. In biotechnology, AI has demonstrated significant potential in drug discovery and development, protein structure prediction, genomic analysis, disease diagnosis, personalised medicine, genetic engineering, and microbial biotechnology. AI-driven computational tools facilitate the identification of potential drug targets, prediction of protein functions, analysis of gene expression patterns, and development of novel therapeutic molecules. Furthermore, AI contributes to agricultural biotechnology, industrial bioprocess optimisation, enzyme engineering, and the development of sustainable biotechnological products. Despite these advances, several challenges limit the widespread implementation of AI in biotechnology. These include the availability and quality of biological datasets, data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, limited model interpretability, high computational requirements, and the need for experimental validation of computational predictions. In addition, ethical considerations, regulatory uncertainties, and the lack of interdisciplinary expertise present significant barriers to practical applications. Future developments are expected to focus on integrating AI with multi-omics technologies, automation, high-throughput screening, synthetic biology, and laboratory robotics. Generative AI and advanced predictive models may further accelerate biological discovery and enable the design of proteins, enzymes, and therapeutics with improved properties. Responsible AI development, transparent algorithms, standardised datasets, and collaboration between computational scientists and experimental biologists will be essential for translating AI-driven predictions into reliable biological applications. This mini-review highlights the current applications of AI in biotechnology, examines the major technical and ethical challenges, and discusses future perspectives for advancing research, innovation, and sustainable biotechnological development.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Discipline Group Development of Traditional Chinese Medicine Institutions: A Quantitative Systematic Review (2023-2025)
items.abstract: This quantitative systematic review analyzes AI applications in discipline group (DG) development of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) institutions, drawing on 372 peer-reviewed studies (98 international, 274 domestic) published 2023-2025. Four author-constructed and validated quantitative indices (TI, RDI, IDI, CKII) were developed to quantify research focus, regional heterogeneity and technical bottlenecks. Five core research themes were identified with quantified TI values: neural network-driven TCM DG structural optimization (0.24), deep learning-based interdisciplinary knowledge integration (0.22), CNN-enhanced clinical-translational synergy (0.18), AI-neural network hybrid TCM talent competency evaluation (0.16), and transformer-based TCM knowledge graph construction (0.08). Quantitative analysis revealed universal low AI model interpretability (mean IDI=0.72), insufficient classical TCM knowledge integration into digital models (mean CKII=0.20), and moderate cross-regional divergence (mean raw RDI=0.082), with knowledge graph research showing the highest divergence (0.254, p=0.012). Targeted recommendations are proposed, including TCM-specific interpretable AI models, unified TCM AI standards, and multi-center validation in vocational/regional TCM institutions. This review offers empirical insights for AI-driven TCM DG optimization, lays a quantitative foundation for TCM digitalization and internationalization, and aligns with China’s 14th Five-Year Plan for TCM Development and WHO’s Global Strategy on Digital Health, boosting its policy relevance and practical value.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in gut-brain axis research for Alzheimer’s disease: From associative insights toward causal inference and personalized interventions
items.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research is shifting from a “brain-centered” model toward a “gut-brain axis system” perspective. However, the causal roles of gut microbiota in AD pathology remain elusive, as traditional association studies struggle to distinguish potential drivers from passengers. This review examines the potential applications and inherent limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in dissecting this complex relationship. We discuss three emerging and conceptually promising directions: First, AI-frameworks for hypothesis-generating causal discovery that can prioritize microbiota-AD relationships for subsequent experimental validation, while recognizing that current approaches predominantly identify statistical associations rather than empirically supported causal conclusions; second, multi-modal fusion networks, when applied with appropriate regularization and validation, can assist in constructing cross-scale molecular maps across microbiota, metabolites, and the brain, though such pathway inferences require careful interpretation as they represent statistical associations rather than biochemically validated mechanisms; and third, the conceptual application of digital twin-based simulation as a long-term vision for personalized microbiota modulation, which currently lacks the ecological resolution and validation required for predictive modeling. By integrating multi-pathway mechanisms of the gut-brain axis and characteristic profiles of gut microbiota, we critically evaluate the technical advantages of machine learning in microbiome data analysis alongside major challenges including overfitting, batch effects, confounding factors, and reproducibility. Leveraging AI-driven microbiota analysis, we propose a phased translational roadmap, from near-term standardization and cross-cohort validation, through mid-term endophenotyping and trial enrichment strategies, to the long-term exploration of personalized interventions, toward the eventual goal of precision prevention. This article outlines a full-cycle framework from discovery to clinical translation and envisions a conceptual ecosystem for future intelligent microecological health management. Achieving the promise of AI-empowered gut-brain axis research will require deep integration across neuroscience, microbiology, computational science, and clinical medicine, alongside rigorous experimental validation, standardized protocols, and realistic appraisal of current technological boundaries.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceuticals: Ethical Risks, Regulatory Challenges, and a Framework for Responsible Governance
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is used in drug discovery, development, manufacturing, medication management, and patient care. These uses differ in supporting evidence and potential harm, so oversight must match their risks. This critical narrative review evaluates selected research, official US and Indian regulatory documents, and international and Indian ethical guidance. Concerns include biased or unrepresentative data, privacy, cybersecurity, unreliable outputs, limited transparency, divided responsibility, staff readiness, and unequal access. Much of the evidence comes from reviews, surveys, interviews, and limited performance tests. US Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) documents emphasize intended use, risk-based evidence of reliability, and lifecycle oversight. Discussion papers, draft guidance, and guiding principles differ from binding requirements. World Health Organization (WHO) and Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) guidance provide ethical foundations, while Indian medical-device rules and Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO) software guidance connect intended use with regulation, local suitability, and monitoring. The review proposes seven governance stages: define intended use; assess risk and responsibilities; manage data and vendors; establish reliability; approve controlled introduction; monitor and manage changes; and address harm or end use. Each stage identifies responsibilities, evidence, and decisions. Assessment also considers human–AI performance, effects across groups, service resilience, and opportunities to question decisions. Responsible pharmaceutical AI requires continuing organizational oversight matched to effects on product quality, regulatory evidence, and patient care.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Governance: Assessing Indonesia's Readiness and Regulatory Framework
items.abstract: Governance constitutes a fundamental component of public administration and plays a decisive role in determiningthe quality, accessibility, and accountability of public services in Indonesia. As social needs and technological capabilitiescontinue to evolve, the government is required to adapt its institutional structures, administrative mechanisms, and regulatoryframeworks to ensure that public services remain effective, inclusive, and responsive. This requirement has become increasinglysignificant following the transformation of conventional government administration toward the Electronic-Based GovernmentSystem (Sistem Pemerintahan Berbasis Elektronik or SPBE). Although digital transformation provides opportunities to improveadministrative efficiency, transparency, and coordination, it also generates new challenges concerning state responsibility, datasovereignty, cybersecurity, personal data protection, and the safeguarding of citizens' rights in cyberspace. These challenges havebecome more complex with the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which enables automated data processing, predictiveanalysis, and decision-support mechanisms within governmental institutions. Accordingly, this study examines the urgency ofgovernmental adaptation and the strategies required to establish AI-based governance that is consistent with the principles oflegality, accountability, transparency, social equity, and public welfare. This research employs a doctrinal legal research methodthrough a literature-based study, utilizing statutory, conceptual, and analytical approaches to examine the relevant legalframework, governance principles, and implications of AI adoption in public administration. The findings indicate that AI offerssubstantial opportunities to improve the efficiency, accuracy, responsiveness, and accessibility of public services. Nevertheless, itsimplementation may also generate algorithmic bias, limited decision-making transparency, cybersecurity vulnerabilities, privacyviolations, and uncertainty regarding legal responsibility for AI-assisted administrative decisions. These risks demonstrate thattechnological advancement alone cannot guarantee the realization of effective and accountable governance. Government readinessmust therefore be strengthened through regulatory adaptation, institutional capacity-building, the development of secure andequitable digital infrastructure, continuous evaluation of AI systems, and meaningful public participation. Furthermore, Indonesiarequires clearer legal standards governing the responsible use of AI, including human oversight, accountability mechanisms, dataprotection, and legal remedies for individuals affected by automated decisions. This study argues that the integration of AI intoSPBE should be understood not merely as a technological modernization initiative but as a legal and institutional transformationthat must remain oriented toward the public interest. Ultimately, adaptive AI-based governance requires a balanced approach thatmaximizes technological benefits while ensuring legal certainty, ethical responsibility, social inclusion, and the protection offundamental rights in Indonesia's evolving digital society.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Tools: Technology Acceptance and Psychological Resilience for Sustainable Mathematics Learning
items.abstract: Mathematics education is being reshaped by artificial intelligence tools, which tailor instruction to individual learners through adaptive guidance and instant feedback, and in doing so can deepen conceptual understanding and build problem-solving capacity. Whether students accept such tools and keep using them, however, rests on a combination of cognitive, behavioral, and psychological conditions. The present study investigated how first-year female undergraduate students (N = 125) at a university in Saudi Arabia accept AI tools, and how psychologically resilient they are, within a mathematics learning environment supported by AI. A further aim was to determine how psychological resilience relates to both technology acceptance and learning engagement in that environment. A model was therefore constructed integrating the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), learning engagement, and psychological resilience. Data was gathered through a quantitative cross-sectional survey at the end of the semester and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Participants reported high technology acceptance and psychological resilience. Model fit was satisfactory, and the proposed hypotheses were supported. Psychological resilience was positively associated with both technology acceptance and learning engagement, and was indirectly associated with behavioral intention through the model’s mediating constructs, of which perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are the first links. By adding psychological resilience and learning engagement to TAM, these findings may broaden the model and help clarify how these constructs relate to AI acceptance in AI-supported mathematics learning.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-based surrogate modeling of hemodynamic indicators in abdominal aortic aneurysms using computational fluid dynamics
items.abstract: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is a progressive dilatative disease of the abdominal aorta with high rupture-related mortality, emphasizing the need for early risk assessment. Conventional anatomical indicators, such as maximum diameter, are insufficient to characterize rupture risk, motivating the incorporation of hemodynamic parameters. Image-based CFD enables the estimation of these parameters but remains clinically limited by high computational cost and long processing times. To overcome these limitations, deep learning–based surrogate models such as MultiViewUNet have recently been proposed, though previous studies were constrained by relatively low spatial resolution and limited coverage of hemodynamic parameters. In this study, we propose MH-UNet, a multi-view, high-resolution surrogate modeling framework that extends the original MultiViewUNet to a higher input resolution and additional hemodynamic parameters. MH-UNet converts three-dimensional AAA geometries into two-dimensional images from multiple viewing angles and predicts TAWSS, OSI, RRT, and ECAP using data from 101 patients. Both single-inference and dual-inference strategies were implemented and compared. Single-inference consistently outperformed dual-inference across all parameters; the cascaded dual-inference scheme amplified errors through the nonlinear OSI and RRT formulations, resulting in negative R² values for OSI, RRT, and ECAP. Among the single-inference predictions, TAWSS was predicted most reliably (R² = 0.803), whereas OSI was the most challenging to predict. Agreement between single-inference predictions and CFD-derived results demonstrates the potential of MH-UNet as a rapid surrogate tool for estimating WSS-derived hemodynamic indices in AAA under fixed boundary conditions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Triage and Diagnostic Support for Gastric Biopsies: A Multi-Centre Prospective Evaluation Across NHS Wales
items.abstract: Background: Histopathology workforce shortages and operational backlogs severely delay gastric cancer reporting. This multi-centre prospective evaluation assessed the diagnostic accuracy, clinical safety-net utility, and workflow triaging efficiency of an artificial intelligence (AI) platform for gastric biopsies across NHS Wales. Methods: A prospective cohort of 848 consecutive gastric biopsy cases across three NHS Health Boards was processed using a commercial AI platform. Diagnostic performance was evaluated against standard-of-care clinical reference diagnoses. Post-analytic cross-tabulation simulated dynamic AI-driven worklist prioritisation to quantify triage safety, false-positive alerts, and turnaround time impact across urgent and routine pathways. Results: For gastric malignancies (n = 40), the AI platform achieved a sensitivity of 100.0% (95% CI: 91.2–100.0%; AUC 0.986) and a specificity of 97.2% (95% CI: 95.8–98.1%). Sensitivities for low-grade dysplasia/adenoma (n = 12) and gastric intestinal metaplasia (n = 98) were 100.0% and 94.9%, respectively. The AI review functioned as a parallel safety net, capturing eight primary lesions missed during routine human evaluation, including one occult adenocarcinoma. In workflow simulation, the platform correctly prioritised 100.0% of cancers, including 6 cancers hidden within routine backlogs, and 97.2% (106/109) of high-risk non-cancer precursors, with false-positive alerts in 4.6% (39/848) of all cases. Conclusions: AI-assisted gastric pathology review demonstrates exceptional diagnostic accuracy, acts as a reliable clinical support tool, and enables effective risk-stratified triage. Deploying AI triage in public healthcare infrastructure offers a scalable solution with the potential to reduce diagnostic backlogs and accelerate treatment for high-risk oncology patients.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Prediction of Adverse Maternal and Perinatal Outcomes: Development and Validation of a Personalized Risk Assessment Model
items.abstract: Background: Adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes are still important causes of morbidity and mortality in the world. Early accurate risk stratification can enhance antenatal care and achieve better pregnancy outcomes. This study set out to create and externally validate an explainable artificial intelligence (AI) based personalised risk assessment tool for predicting adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes. Materials and methods: Between 2020-25, a multicenter retrospective cohort study of 5,248 pregnant women was carried out. Data regarding demographic, clinical, obstetric, laboratory and fetal assessment parameters were retrieved from electronic medical records. The primary outcome was composite outcome which amounted to preeclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, preterm delivery, fetal growth restriction, still birth, admission to the neonatal intensive care unit and perinatal death. Logistic regression, random forest, neural network and XGBoost models were created and evaluated. Both internal and external validation was carried out. SHAP analysis was used to measure the interpretability of models. Results: There were 1,162 pregnancies with adverse outcomes (22.1%). XGBoost demonstrated the best performance with an AUROC of 0.914 (95% CI: 0.899–0.928), sensitivity of 87.6%, specificity of 86.9%, and F1-score of 0.84. Fetal growth parameters, previous preeclampsia, fasting plasma glucose, body mass index, maternal age and systolic blood pressure were the most influential predictors. External validation demonstrated excellent AUROC (0.908) and slope (0.96) measures of discrimination and calibration, respectively. Conclusion: The interpretable model built with artificial intelligence was able to successfully forecast adverse maternal and perinatal outcomes, and had high generalizability. It could be combined into the regular antenatal manager to help tailor risk stratification and preventive measures. items.abstract: Biomarkers are measurable biological characteristics that can support disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection, and monitoring oftherapeutic response. Their discovery increasingly depends on high-dimensional and heterogeneous data such as genomics, transcriptomics,proteomics, medical imaging, electronic health records, and wearable-device measurements. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help identifypatterns across these sources and support more efficient clinical-trial planning, including patient stratification, eligibility screening, recruitmentforecasting, endpoint assessment, and risk monitoring. This paper presents a conceptual framework connecting AI-enabled biomarker discoverywith clinical-trial optimization. The framework covers data governance, preprocessing, multimodal feature integration, candidate selection,validation, trial feasibility, and continuous monitoring. It emphasizes that computational performance alone does not establish clinicalusefulness: candidate biomarkers require independent replication, analytical validation, clinical validation, and evidence of utility in a clearlydefined context of use. The paper synthesizes published literature and regulatory principles; it does not report a newly conducted clinical studyor claim original performance results. Responsible implementation requires privacy protection, representative data, transparent documentation,clinician oversight, and prospective evaluation before AI outputs influence patient care.

items.title: Assessing Fitness to Work
items.abstract: This chapter positions fitness-to-work assessment as a central mechanism for sustaining work participation against a backdrop of rising ill health-related inactivity, workforce shortages and increasing policy emphasis on early intervention. It outlines the key UK policy, legal and economic drivers, including fit note reform, employer duties under health and safety legislation, and evidence showing that good work supports health, to explain why fitness-to-work decisions must be timely, functional and specific to the demands of the job. The distinct roles of general practice and occupational health are clarified, highlighting occupational health’s unique impartiality and its capacity to integrate job requirements, risk controls and clinical status into defensible fitness-to-work opinions. Building on this context, the chapter presents a practical biopsychosocial functional framework for fitness-to-work assessment. It shows how practitioners can evaluate task-relevant capability, synthesise findings, and identify which biological, psychological and organisational factors are modifiable. Core levers for change are introduced alongside outcome measures that support structured review, with examples demonstrating how biopsychosocial formulation can directly inform fitness-to-work decisions and proportionate, time-bound adjustments. The chapter concludes with a step-by-step consultation structure that turns principles into practice, offering practitioners a transparent, defensible and consistently applicable method for delivering high-quality fitness-to-work assessments.

items.title: Assessing Mental Health and Suicide Risk at Work
items.abstract: This chapter addresses one of the most sensitive areas in occupational health practice: supporting employees who are experiencing depression and assessing concerns about suicide. It begins by exploring how depressive symptoms influence work participation, functional capacity and decision-making, and how workplace pressures may contribute to the onset or worsening of mental distress. It also outlines how occupational health practitioners can support safe work retention and facilitate a sustainable return to work. The chapter then describes a structured approach to mental health assessment using validated tools such as the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 and the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. These instruments inform, but do not determine, clinical reasoning. A formulation-led method is presented that reflects contemporary guidance promoting personalised assessment, collaborative safety planning and a move away from predictive or stratified risk approaches. Finally, the chapter considers the emotional impact of repeated exposure to distress on occupational health practitioners. It highlights the importance of supervision, reflective practice and structured decompression as preventive supports. The aim is to provide clear, evidence-informed guidance to strengthen assessment, communication, documentation and practitioner well-being within occupational health practice.
